messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Babies): Babies, Public Transport: Bus riding, Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ethan was twenty-three when it happened, a fisherman out of Gloucester whose work had always meant early mornings alone on the water. One night he was ambushed on his own boat by four men who had come for his catch and the cash he kept in a waterproof box. They didn’t just take the money. They bound his wrists behind his back with zip ties, forced him to kneel on the deck, and spent hours methodically breaking him with a tire iron and a knife. The pain was sharpest in his ribs and across his palms where they had pressed the blade flat, showing him they could do worse. Through it all, one of the men had a baby monitor clipped to his belt, and from its speaker came the thin, pulsing cry of an infant—a sound that cut through the ocean noise and lodged itself in Ethan’s memory. When they finally left him, bleeding and tied to the mast, he had to wait until dawn before another boat spotted him.

In the three years since, Ethan has learned to live around the memory, but the memory has not learned to live quietly inside him. The rage that comes when he thinks of those men is a hot, shaking thing—he once punched a hole in his kitchen drywall just from replaying their laughter. But worse than the rage is the way his body betrays him. When a memory surfaces, he feels his arms wrenched behind his back, his knees pressed hard against a cold surface, even if he is standing in his own living room. The same ribs ache, the same palms burn, and no amount of stretching or painkillers makes it stop. He has come to believe that his body is still in that moment, and that the men might still be in the world, maybe even looking for him again.

He now sleeps with his back pressed against the headboard so he can see the bedroom door. He has stopped taking the bus into town because the closed space and the strangers’ shoulders trigger the sense of being trapped, and he has to get off before his next stop, heart pounding, convinced he hears the squeal of the baby monitor. The first time he heard a real baby cry in a grocery store, he dropped a jar of pickles and walked out without paying. He does not tell his wife, Maria, the full reason for these behaviors. When she asks why he stiffens when she touches his shoulder from behind, he says he’s just jumpy. But the truth is that feeling emotionally vulnerable—letting her see his fear or his grief—feels as dangerous as kneeling on that deck. He is certain that if he lets down his guard, something terrible will follow.

His vigilance has become a habit he cannot shake. In any room, he scans for potential weapons: a fire extinguisher, a heavy lamp, a pair of scissors left on the counter. He listens for footsteps when Maria is at work, tuning in to creaks in the hallway, the click of a lock, anything that might mean someone is coming inside. He has told himself this is just being prepared, but he knows it is a lie. He is waiting for the next attack. His marriage has begun to fray—Maria feels locked out, and she has stopped asking him to go to dinner with friends because he insists on sitting with his back to the wall and will not explain why.

What finally brings Ethan to the clinic is a morning on his own boat, the only place he still feels somewhat safe. He was hauling traps when a buoy line tangled, and for a few seconds his arm was pinned. The sudden restraint, the pressure on his wrist, sent him into a full reenactment: he collapsed onto the deck, his body rigid in the same kneeling position, his ribs aching, and he heard the baby crying from nowhere. He lay there for five minutes, trembling with rage and pain, before he could stand. That night, he told Maria he needed help. He is afraid of what his anger might make him do, but more than that, he is afraid that the men are still out there, and that he will never stop listening for a sound that ended years ago. He hopes, quietly, that talking about it might release his body from the position it has held for so long.
